guide.summary: Dropbox uses a standard authorization code flow with optional PKCE and refresh tokens, which you get only if you request offline access. Creating an app is quick. The hard part is the production gate. A new app is in development status and limited to 500 linked users. Dropbox will not review it until it has 50 linked users, and once it reaches 50 you have two weeks to get approved before new linking freezes. How long review takes is not documented.
auth_alternatives: Generated access token: choose it only for testing against your own Dropbox account. It cannot be used for other users.
Pre-built components (Chooser, Saver, Embedder): choose them if file picking, saving or embedding is enough. They need no production approval, but they are not general API access for an agent.

reasons_to_bring_own: Your own app gets up to 500 development users, but once it links 50 users you have two weeks to win production approval or linking freezes. Plan for that before you switch.
If your product is a developer tool that wraps the Dropbox platform, Dropbox requires each of your developers to have their own app key.
You control the requested scopes and content access (App Folder or Full Dropbox). Dropbox reviews these for overly broad permissions.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth; you do not need your own app yet because a self-built Dropbox app must reach 50 linked users before Dropbox will review it for production, then must be approved within two weeks or new linking freezes, unless you are building a developer tool, where Dropbox requires each developer to have their own app key.

app_specific_gotchas.text: You get no refresh token unless you add token_access_type=offline to the authorization URL. Without it, your agent loses access when the short-lived token expires.
Reaching 50 users starts a two-week clock, and missing it freezes new linking. Unlinking users does not reset it.
The app name cannot be changed once the app has production status.
Changing scopes on the Permissions tab does not affect existing access tokens. Users must re-authorize to pick up new scopes.
Developer tools that wrap the Dropbox platform must have each of their developers use their own app key.

steps.title: Decide content access and integration shape
steps.detail_md:
Two choices to make before creating the app.

**Content access: App Folder or Full Dropbox.** The create-app form asks for this.
- App Folder is narrower.
- Full Dropbox is broader.
- Dropbox reviews production requests for overly broad permissions, and asking for more scope or content access than you need may affect review.
- Pick the narrowest option that works for your agent. The agent can lay out the trade-off, but you make the call.
- Whether this choice can be changed after creation is not documented, so treat it as a real decision.

**Pre-built components.** If you only need the Chooser, Saver or Embedder, those do not need production approval. That may save you the whole review path.

**Developer tools.** If your product is a developer tool that wraps the Dropbox platform, each of your developers needs their own app key. Do not plan on a single shared key in that case.

steps.title: Draft redirect URIs, scope list, app name options and privacy policy
steps.detail_md:
The agent prepares the inputs you will paste into the console.

- **Redirect URIs:** the exact list for each environment. Dropbox matches them exactly at authorization time.
- **Scope list:** the minimal set your features need.
- **App name candidates:** the name cannot be changed once the app has production status.
- **Privacy policy draft:** Dropbox expects a policy specific to this app.

steps.title: Create the app in the Dropbox Developer Console
steps.detail_md:
Log in at https://www.dropbox.com/developers and create a new app.

- Choose **Scoped access** as the API type.
- Choose the content access type you decided on in step 1.
- Enter the app name.
- Tick the **API Terms and Conditions** box. The app cannot be created without it.

The new app starts in development status.

steps.title: Copy the app key and secret
steps.detail_md: The app key is your `client_id` and the app secret is your `client_secret`. Store them in your secrets manager. Do not put them in code.

steps.title: Register redirect URIs
steps.detail_md:
On the **Settings** tab, open the **OAuth 2** section and add every redirect URI from step 2.

- Each one must exactly match the `redirect_uri` your code sends.
- `redirect_uri` is technically optional with the code flow, but then the user has to copy and paste the code by hand. That is not suitable for an agent.

steps.title: Decide on the Allow public clients toggle
steps.detail_md:
One toggle in the OAuth 2 settings controls both the legacy implicit grant and PKCE.

- **Enable it** only if part of your integration runs without a secret (for example a mobile or browser client using PKCE).
- **Leave it off** for a server-side agent that keeps the secret.

steps.title: Select scopes on the Permissions tab and save
steps.detail_md:
Tick the minimal scopes from step 2 and save.

- Saved changes do not affect access tokens that already exist. Users will need to re-authorize to pick up new scopes.
- Overly broad permissions are a review concern.

steps.title: Write the OAuth integration code
steps.detail_md:
Use the authorization code flow, which Dropbox recommends for all app types.

- **Authorize:** send users to `https://www.dropbox.com/oauth2/authorize` with `response_type=code`.
- **Offline access:** add `token_access_type=offline`, otherwise no refresh token is returned.
- **Token exchange:** call `/oauth2/token`. Dropbox's example uses `https://api.dropbox.com/oauth2/token`.
- **PKCE (if public clients are on):** use S256, with a `code_verifier` of 43 to 128 permitted characters.
- **Expiry:** access tokens are short-lived. Read the expiry from the token response rather than hardcoding it.
- **Refresh tokens:** they do not expire automatically, but they can be revoked. Handle revocation by re-prompting the user.

Note that the discovery document does not advertise PKCE methods, so do not rely on discovery for that.

Alternatively, Composio lists Dropbox with managed auth, if you would rather not run this flow yourself.

steps.title: Test against your own account
steps.detail_md:
Run the full OAuth flow with your own Dropbox account. A development-status app can link your account without extra setup.

- The console's generated access token is handy for quick API checks against your account.
- It cannot be used for other users, so it does not prove your OAuth flow works.
- An invalid `client_id` sends the browser to an authorize_error page. If you see one, check the key first.

steps.title: Enable additional development users
steps.detail_md:
To let testers or early users connect, enable extra development users on the app's **Settings** tab.

- A development-status app can link at most 500 Dropbox users in total.
- Read step 12 before opening this up widely. A two-week clock starts at 50 linked users.

steps.title: Prepare production prerequisites
steps.detail_md:
Get these in place before you apply.

- **App icon:** add it on the **Branding** tab. It is required before you can apply for production.
- **Privacy policy:** publish the app-specific policy drafted in step 2.
- **Compliance:** check against the branding guidelines and terms and conditions. Apps that violate them are rejected.

steps.title: Reach 50 linked users and track the two-week clock
steps.detail_md:
Dropbox will not review a production app until it has linked at least 50 users.

- Once you pass 50, you have two weeks to get production approval. After that, linking new users is frozen.
- A frozen app can only be unfrozen by getting production approval. Unlinking users does not help.
- Have step 11 finished before you cross 50, and apply right away.

How long it takes to reach 50 depends on your adoption. The estimate here only covers setting up a linked-user count alert.

steps.title: Confirm the final app name and apply for production
steps.detail_md:
1. Confirm the app name is final. It cannot be changed once the app has production status.
2. Click **Apply for production** in the **App configuration** section of the **Settings** tab.

steps.title: Dropbox production review
steps.detail_md:
Dropbox reviews the request, including checking for overly broad permissions and compliance with the branding guidelines and terms.

- How long review takes is not documented.
- The minute estimate is 0 because the duration is unknown, not because review is instant.
- Your two-week window from step 12 keeps running during review.

steps.title: Open the integration to all users
steps.detail_md: After production approval, any number of Dropbox users can link to the app. Remove any tester-only gating from your onboarding.

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, Dropbox requires app review for production use so that any Dropbox user can connect, since apps start in development mode restricted to the developer's own account and a limited set of users.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm new apps start in development status limited to the developer's own account plus enabled additional users, and that after production approval any number of Dropbox users can link; they do not explicitly state that review is required for arbitrary users, but production approval is what unlocks unlimited linking.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Dropbox app review typically takes about 5 business days, though I'd say it commonly completes within 2 to 4 weeks.
belief_diff.finding: The claims give no typical review duration; they only state a two-week window after reaching 50 linked users to get production approval, which is a deadline rather than a review time.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: Unapproved development-status apps are limited to 500 users total, with no more than 1 team and only the developer's own linked accounts ahead of approval.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm development-status apps can link at most 500 users in total and can link only the developer's own account unless additional users are enabled; the claims do not mention a team limit of 1.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Creating and using a Dropbox app is free, with no fee charged for API access at standard usage levels.
belief_diff.finding: The claims do not address pricing or fees.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: Dropbox requires a privacy policy URL and a clear description of data use for review, but does not require business verification, a custom domain, or a demo video.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say an app-specific privacy policy is expected and an app icon must be added before applying, plus accepting Terms and Conditions; they do not address business verification, custom domain, or demo video, and do not mention a data-use description.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Redirect URIs must be registered exactly in the app console, must use HTTPS except for localhost during development, and must match the requested URI character for character.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm redirect URIs must be registered exactly in the Developer Console (OAuth 2 section of Settings) and must exactly match the redirect_uri at authorization time; the HTTPS and localhost rules are not addressed, and redirect_uri is optional with the code flow.
